qs.q: A complication of Streptococcus pharyngitis (strep throat) is acute rheumatic fever, an inflammatory condition affecting the heart, joints, brain, and skin.
qs.e: Acute rheumatic fever is a well-established non-suppurative sequela of untreated or inadequately treated group A streptococcal pharyngitis. The other options can also be associated with streptococcal infections, but rheumatic fever is a classic complication.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rheumatic fever is an autoimmune inflammation of the heart, joints, skin, and nervous system that follows untreated Group A streptococcal throat infection, mainly in children. Prompt recognition using the Jones criteria and secondary prophylaxis prevent permanent heart damage.

sections.p: Acute rheumatic fever (ARF) is a post‑streptococcal immune reaction causing multi‑system inflammation. Diagnosis relies on the Jones criteria, which combine major and minor clinical findings with evidence of recent streptococcal infection.
b: Major: migratory polyarthritis, carditis, chorea, erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules.
Minor: fever, arthralgia, elevated ESR/CRP, prolonged PR interval.

t.b: Does the patient have recent streptococcal exposure? High titres support recent infection.

t.a: Throat culture or rapid antigen test
t.b: Is there a current streptococcal throat infection? Positive test confirms active infection; negative does not rule out prior infection.

sections.p: Severity is graded by cardiac involvement: mild (isolated valvulitis), moderate (murmur with heart failure signs), severe (heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or severe valvular regurgitation). Neurologic chorea is staged by functional impact.
b: Mild: no heart failure, normal ventricular function.
Moderate: mild heart failure, NYHA I‑II.
Severe: overt heart failure, NYHA III‑IV, or severe valve disease.

sections.p: The trigger is a recent Group A Streptococcus (GAS) pharyngitis, especially in settings with limited access to antibiotics. Other infections are rarely implicated.
b: Group A Streptococcus pharyngitis (most common).
Concurrent skin infection with GAS (rare).
In low‑resource settings, poor treatment adherence and crowded living conditions increase risk.

sections.p: Patients, usually 5‑15 years old, develop fever, migratory polyarthritis, and a new heart murmur. Skin findings (erythema marginatum, subcutaneous nodules) and neurologic chorea may appear days to weeks after the sore throat.
b: Migratory arthritis affecting large joints, resolves within weeks.
Carditis: new regurgitant murmur, pericardial rub, or heart failure.
Sydenham chorea: involuntary movements, emotional lability.

sections.p: Investigations confirm recent streptococcal infection, assess cardiac involvement, and rule out mimics.
b: ECG for PR prolongation, arrhythmias.
Echocardiography to detect valvulitis, regurgitation, or pericardial effusion.

t.b: Is there evidence of carditis? PR prolongation or arrhythmia suggests myocardial involvement.
What is the extent of valvular damage? Detects regurgitation, thickening, or reduced function.
Are inflammatory markers elevated? Supports active inflammation; normal does not exclude ARF.

sections.p: Uncontrolled carditis can rapidly progress to heart failure, severe mitral or aortic regurgitation, and permanent rheumatic heart disease.
b: Sudden dyspnea, pulmonary edema, or hypotension.
New or worsening murmur with signs of heart failure.
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to care for self.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection, suppress inflammation, and protect the heart. Use anti‑inflammatory agents and secondary prophylaxis to prevent recurrence.
b: Penicillin (or amoxicillin) for 10 days to eradicate GAS; chosen for narrow spectrum and safety.
Aspirin (high‑dose) for anti‑inflammatory effect; avoids steroids unless severe carditis.
Corticosteroids for severe carditis or refractory inflammation; avoid if mild disease.
Heart failure therapy (diuretics, ACE‑inhibitors) when indicated.

sections.p: Long‑term secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin G prevents recurrence and progression to rheumatic heart disease. Follow cardiac status with periodic echocardiography.
b: Monthly benzathine penicillin G for at least 10 years or until age 21, whichever is longer.
Echocardiogram at 6 months, then yearly if valve disease persists.
Educate families about early treatment of sore throat.

sections.p: Conditions that mimic ARF include septic arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis, viral myocarditis, and systemic lupus erythematosus.
b: Septic arthritis: usually single joint, high fever, positive joint fluid culture.
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: chronic, not linked to recent strep.
Viral myocarditis: lacks migratory arthritis and streptococcal evidence.

sections.p: Normal ASO titres can occur if the infection was > 8 weeks ago or if the patient is a poor antibody responder; a negative throat culture does not exclude prior infection.
b: ASO may be low in early infection; repeat testing after 2 weeks if suspicion remains.
CRP/ESR can be modestly raised in other inflammatory conditions.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden shortness of breath or chest pain
Rapidly worsening heart murmur with signs of heart failure
Severe chorea causing injury or inability to eat

faq.q: Why does a throat infection cause heart damage?
faq.a: Molecular mimicry makes antibodies against streptococcal antigens cross‑react with cardiac tissue, leading to inflammation.
No; only the streptococcal infection is contagious, not the autoimmune reaction.
It is rare but can occur, especially in those with untreated strep infections or poor access to care.
